claim: Cortical oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) arise from medial ganglionic eminence (MGE), lateral/caudal ganglionic eminence (LGE/CGE), and cortical radial glial cells (RGCs).
source: It is widely accepted that cortical oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) arise from medial ganglionic eminence (MGE), lateral/caudal ganglionic eminence (LGE/CGE), and cortical radial glial cells (RGCs).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field, representing the widely accepted view prior to the current study's findings.

claim: The LGE/CGE does not give rise to cortical OPCs.
source: Furthermore, we used a Cre/loxP-dependent exclusion strategy to reveal that the LGE/CGE does not give rise to cortical OPCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using a Cre/loxP-dependent exclusion strategy described in the manuscript.

claim: Specifically eliminating MGE-derived OPCs leads to a significant reduction of cortical OPCs.
source: Additionally, we showed that specifically eliminating MGE-derived OPCs leads to a significant reduction of cortical OPCs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Olig2 conditional knockout mice (Nkx2.1Cre; Olig2F/F mice).

claim: Oligodendrocytes are one of the most abundant cell types in the mammalian neocortex.
source: Oligodendrocytes (OLs) are one of the most abundant cell types in the mammalian neocortex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about oligodendrocytes in the neocortex.

claim: The emergence of myelination OLs in vertebrates is a major event in the evolution of the central nervous system (CNS).
source: The emergence of myelination OLs in vertebrates is a major event in the evolution of the central nervous system (CNS), as these cells play a crucial role in enhancing axonal insulation and the conduction of neural impulses.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the evolutionary significance of myelinating oligodendrocytes.

claim: Myelin loss or dysfunction is associated with many disorders, such as multiple sclerosis, depression, and pediatric leukodystrophies.
source: Myelin loss or dysfunction is associated with many disorders, such as multiple sclerosis, depression, and pediatric leukodystrophies (Goldman et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goldman et al., 2021 and Zhou et al., 2021.

claim: OPCs proliferate and migrate away from the ventricular germinal zone (VZ) into developing gray and white matter before differentiating into mature OLs.
source: OPCs proliferate and migrate away from the ventricular germinal zone (VZ) into developing gray and white matter before differentiating into mature OLs (Miller, 1996; Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miller, 1996 and Huang et al., 2020.

claim: Cortical OPCs are generated in three waves, starting with a ventral wave, gradually transitioning to more dorsal origins.
source: A landmark study Kessaris et al., 2006 demonstrated that cortical OPCs are generated in three waves, starting with a ventral wave, gradually transitioning to more dorsal origins.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kessaris et al., 2006.

claim: The first wave of cortical OPCs is derived from the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE) or the anterior entopeduncular area (AEP) at embryonic day 12.5 (E12.5) (Nkx2.1+ lineage).
source: The first wave of cortical OPCs is derived from the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE) or the anterior entopeduncular area (AEP) at embryonic day 12.5 (E12.5) (Nkx2.1+ lineage).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge from previous studies about the developmental origins of cortical OPCs.

claim: The second wave of cortical OLs is derived from the lateral/caudal ganglionic eminences (LGE/CGE) at E15.5 (Gsx2+/Nkx2.1- lineage).
source: The second wave of cortical OLs is derived from the lateral/caudal ganglionic eminences (LGE/CGE) at E15.5 (Gsx2+/Nkx2.1- lineage).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge from previous studies about the developmental origins of cortical OPCs.

claim: The final wave of OPCs occurs at P0, when OPCs originate from cortical glial progenitor cells (Emx1+ lineage).
source: The final wave occurs at P0, when OPCs originate from cortical glial progenitor cells (Emx1+ lineage).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge from previous studies about the developmental origins of cortical OPCs.

claim: Cortical glial progenitor cells were found to express Gsx2 after E16.5.
source: Our recent studies (Li et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020), however, challenge the notion that cortical OLs are generated in these three waves (Kessaris et al., 2006; Richardson et al., 2006; Rowitch and Kriegstein, 2010; Bergles and Richardson, 2015), as the cortical glial progenitor cells were also found to express Gsx2, which was known to be exclusively expressed in the developing subpallium (Chapman et al., 2018; Chapman et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2021), after E16.5 (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2021 and Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: Gsx2 was known to be exclusively expressed in the developing subpallium.
source: Our recent studies (Li et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020), however, challenge the notion that cortical OLs are generated in these three waves (Kessaris et al., 2006; Richardson et al., 2006; Rowitch and Kriegstein, 2010; Bergles and Richardson, 2015), as the cortical glial progenitor cells were also found to express Gsx2, which was known to be exclusively expressed in the developing subpallium (Chapman et al., 2018; Chapman et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2021), after E16.5 (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chapman et al., 2018; Chapman et al., 2013; and Wen et al., 2021.

claim: Gsx2+/Nkx2.1- lineage OLs may not represent LGE-derived cortical OLs.
source: Therefore, Gsx2+/Nkx2.1- lineage OLs may not represent LGE-derived cortical OLs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that cortical glial progenitor cells express Gsx2 after E16.5.

claim: There was no observable Pdgfra+ cell migration stream from the LGE to the cortex from E13.5 to postnatal day 0 (P0).
source: Our results showed that there was no observable Pdgfra+ cell migration stream from the LGE to the cortex from E13.5 to postnatal day 0 (P0) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: LGE-derived cells expressing tdTomato were observed throughout the whole LGE (striatum) at E18.5.
source: Interestingly, we observed many tdT+ cells throughout the whole LGE (striatum) at E18.5.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from in utero electroporation experiments.

claim: There were very few tdT+ cells detected in the cortex at E18.5 following LGE electroporation.
source: In contrast, there were very few tdT+ cells detected in the cortex (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: OPCs express Olig2, Sox10, Pdgfra, and NG2 (Cspg4).
source: OPCs express Olig2, Sox10, Pdgfra, and NG2 (Cspg4) and mature neurons express NeuN (Sun et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 2001; Lu et al., 2002; Finzsch et al., 2008; Reiprich et al., 2017; Kucharova and Stallcup, 2010; Sánchez-González et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to Sun et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 2001; Lu et al., 2002; Finzsch et al., 2008; Reiprich et al., 2017; Kucharova and Stallcup, 2010; Sánchez-González et al., 2020.

claim: Mature neurons express NeuN.
source: OPCs express Olig2, Sox10, Pdgfra, and NG2 (Cspg4) and mature neurons express NeuN (Sun et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 2001; Lu et al., 2002; Finzsch et al., 2008; Reiprich et al., 2017; Kucharova and Stallcup, 2010; Sánchez-González et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to Sun et al., 2001; Zhou et al., 2001; Lu et al., 2002; Finzsch et al., 2008; Reiprich et al., 2017; Kucharova and Stallcup, 2010; Sánchez-González et al., 2020.

claim: tdT+ cells in the cortex did not express OPC marker genes but expressed NeuN.
source: Within the cortex, tdT+ cells did not express OPC marker genes but express NeuN; however, tdT+ cells expressed OPC marker genes and NeuN in the striatum (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: tdT+ cells in the striatum expressed OPC marker genes and NeuN.
source: Within the cortex, tdT+ cells did not express OPC marker genes but express NeuN; however, tdT+ cells expressed OPC marker genes and NeuN in the striatum (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: LGE progenitors generate striatum OLs and astrocytes at P49.
source: Our results showed that LGE progenitors generate striatum OLs and astrocytes, which expressed SOX10 and SOX9, respectively (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G from IUE experiments at P0 analyzed at P49.

claim: At P10, the majority of the tdT+ cells were located in the striatum, whereas very few tdT+ cells were located in the neocortex.
source: We observed that at P10, the majority of the tdT+ cells were located in the striatum, whereas very few tdT+ cells were located in the neocortex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: All tdT+ cells in the neocortex expressed NeuN but did not express OLIG2 at P10.
source: All tdT+ cells in the neocortex expressed NeuN but did not express OLIG2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: tdT+ cells in the neocortex did not express OPC marker genes; instead, they expressed NeuN.
source: In fact, tdT+ cells in the neocortex did not express OPC marker genes; instead, they expressed NeuN in the neocortex.
evidence: This is based on immunostaining data from the experiments.

claim: tdT+ cells in the striatum expressed OPC marker genes (Olig2, Sox10, and Pdgfra) and NeuN at P10.
source: In contrast, tdT+ cells in the striatum expressed OPC marker genes (Olig2, Sox10, and Pdgfra) and NeuN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D), consistent with our observation at E18.5 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: tdT+ cells expressed the astrocyte marker ALDH1L1 in the striatum at P10.
source: We also found that tdT+ cells expressed the astrocyte marker ALDH1L1 in the striatum at P10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The traced cells tended to be localized in the striatum based on 3D reconstruction.
source: Furthermore, through consecutive tissue sectioning and 3D reconstruction, we revealed that the traced cells tended to be localized in the striatum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D reconstruction data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The LGE gives rise to striatal OLs, neurons, and astrocytes, but not cortical OLs.
source: Collectively, our findings indicated that the LGE gives rise to striatal OLs, neurons, and astrocytes, but not cortical OLs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations using IUE and fate mapping.

claim: Most traced cells (GFP+) using the PiggyBac transposon system were located in the striatum, and very few traced cells were observed in the cortex at E18.5.
source: In this system, most traced cells (GFP+) were located in the striatum, and very few traced cells were observed in the cortex (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and E using the PiggyBac transposon system.

claim: A small population of RGCs located in the dorsal LGE or lateral/ventral pallium was labeled by IUE.
source: Usually, a small population of RGCs located in the dorsal LGE or lateral/ventral pallium was labeled by IUE.
evidence: This is an observation from the IUE experiments.

claim: RGCs labeled in the dorsal LGE or lateral/ventral pallium mainly migrated to the lateral/ventral pallium and amygdala.
source: These RGCs mainly migrated to the lateral/ventral pallium and amygdala (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No GFP+ cells that were OPCs were observed in the dorsal cortex, as these cells did not express OLIG2, SOX10, or PDGFRA.
source: We did not observe any GFP+ cells that were OPCs in the dorsal cortex, as these cells did not express OLIG2, SOX10, or PDGFRA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GFP+ cells in the dorsal cortex expressed NeuN.
source: Instead, they expressed NeuN (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GFP+ cells expressed OLIG2, SOX10, PDGFRA, and NeuN in the striatum at E18.5.
source: In contrast, GFP+ cells expressed OLIG2, SOX10, PDGFRA, and NeuN in the striatum at E18.5 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Many GSX2+ cells were located in the cortical SVZ in Emx1Cre; H2B-GFP mice.
source: To confirm these findings, using the Emx1Cre; H2B-GFP mice, we found that many GSX2+ cells were located in the cortical SVZ.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Emx1Cre; H2B-GFP mice.

claim: GSX2+ cells in the cortical SVZ were co-labeled with GFP (Emx1+ lineage).
source: Interestingly, these GSX2+ cells were co-labeled with GFP (Emx1+ lineage), suggesting that the cortical SVZ GSX2+ cells were derived from the cortical progenitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Cortical SVZ GSX2+ cells were derived from the cortical progenitors.
source: Interestingly, these GSX2+ cells were co-labeled with GFP (Emx1+ lineage), suggesting that the cortical SVZ GSX2+ cells were derived from the cortical progenitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-labeling of GSX2+ cells with GFP in Emx1Cre; H2B-GFP mice.

claim: Emx1Cre was specifically expressed in cortical RGCs.
source: Because Emx1Cre was specifically expressed in cortical RGCs (Gorski et al., 2002) and Nkx2.1Cre was specifically expressed in MGE/AEP RGCs (Xu et al., 2008), cortical OPCs were traced (GFP+ cells) in using Emx1Cre; Nkx2.1Cre; H2B-GFP mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gorski et al., 2002.

claim: Nkx2.1Cre was specifically expressed in MGE/AEP RGCs.
source: Because Emx1Cre was specifically expressed in cortical RGCs (Gorski et al., 2002) and Nkx2.1Cre was specifically expressed in MGE/AEP RGCs (Xu et al., 2008), cortical OPCs were traced (GFP+ cells) in using Emx1Cre; Nkx2.1Cre; H2B-GFP mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2008.

claim: The majority of OPCs or OLs were co-labeled with GFP in Emx1Cre; Nkx2.1Cre; H2B-GFP mice at P10.
source: We observed that the majority of OPCs or OLs were co-labeled with GFP in Emx1Cre; Nkx2.1Cre; H2B-GFP mice at P10 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Only approximately 2% of OPCs were GFP- cells at P10, and they were possibly derived from the LGE/CGE.
source: Statistical analysis showed that only approximately 2% of OPCs were GFP- cells, and they were possibly derived from the LGE/CGE (Figure 3D and E), which was consistent with our observation at P0 (Figure 3G–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Many GFP+ cells expressed SOX10 and PDGFRA in the striatum at P10.
source: We also found that many GFP+ cells expressed SOX10 and PDGFRA in the striatum at P10 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The expression of Nkx2.1Cre is lower within the dorsalmost region of the MGE than in other Nkx2.1-expressing regions.
source: Importantly, the expression of Nkx2.1Cre is lower within the dorsalmost region of the MGE than in other Nkx2.1-expressing regions (Xu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2008.

claim: GFP- OPCs (~2%) may be derived from the dorsal MGE rather than from the LGE/CGE.
source: Thus, these GFP- OPCs (~2%) may be derived from the dorsal MGE rather than from the LGE/CGE.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the lower expression of Nkx2.1Cre in the dorsalmost MGE.

claim: Nearly all cortical OLs/OPCs were derived from MGE/AEP and cortical RGCs.
source: Using this approach, we revealed that nearly all cortical OLs/OPCs were derived from MGE/AEP and cortical RGCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the exclusion strategy experiments.

claim: The contribution of cortical OPCs from the LGE/CGE is minimal.
source: Taken together, our findings indicated that the contribution of cortical OPCs from the LGE/CGE is minimal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental approaches.

claim: Olig2 plays a critical role in the regulation of OPC fate determination.
source: Olig2, a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, plays a critical role in the regulation of OPC fate determination.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the role of Olig2.

claim: MGE/AEP-derived OPCs migrate into the cortex around E14.5.
source: A previous study (Kessaris et al., 2006) showed that MGE/AEP-derived OPCs migrate into the cortex around E14.5, and LGE/CGE-derived OPCs migrate into cortex around E15.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kessaris et al., 2006.

claim: LGE/CGE-derived OPCs migrate into cortex around E15.5.
source: A previous study (Kessaris et al., 2006) showed that MGE/AEP-derived OPCs migrate into the cortex around E14.5, and LGE/CGE-derived OPCs migrate into cortex around E15.5.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kessaris et al., 2006.

claim: The expression of OPC marker genes, such as Sox10 and Pdgfra, was significantly reduced (>10-fold) in the cortex of Olig2-NCKO mice, compared to the control mice at E14.5 and E16.5.
source: Our results showed that the expression of OPC marker genes, such as Sox10 and Pdgfra, was significantly reduced (>10-fold) in the cortex of Olig2-NCKO mice, compared to the control mice at E14.5 and E16.5 (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C–E from Olig2-NCKO mice.

claim: Few PDGFRA-positive cells were detected in the MGE/AEP of the Olig2-NCKO mice.
source: Indeed, we observed few PDGFRA-positive cells in the MGE/AEP of the Olig2-NCKO mice (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The MGE/AEP was the predominant ventral source of cortical OPCs.
source: Altogether, our findings indicated that the MGE/AEP was the predominant ventral source of cortical OPCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Olig2-NCKO mouse experiments.

claim: Cortical OLs are heterogeneous, as there are transcriptionally distinct subpopulations of cortical OLs during development and disease.
source: Recent studies have shown that cortical OLs are heterogeneous, as there are transcriptionally distinct subpopulations of cortical OLs during development and disease (Marques et al., 2018; Floriddia et al., 2020; Marques et al., 2016; Falcão et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marques et al., 2018; Floriddia et al., 2020; Marques et al., 2016; and Falcão et al., 2018.

claim: OLs are derived from distinct OPC pools, which acquire different abilities to respond to demyelination.
source: Indeed, OLs are derived from distinct OPC pools, which acquire different abilities to respond to demyelination (Kessaris et al., 2006; Crawford et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kessaris et al., 2006 and Crawford et al., 2016.

claim: The specification of OLs depends on SHH protein released from the notochord and floor plate.
source: In general, the specification of OLs depends on SHH protein released from the notochord and floor plate, as Shh expression is both necessary and sufficient for OL generation in the spinal cord (Orentas et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Orentas et al., 1999.

claim: Shh expression is both necessary and sufficient for OL generation in the spinal cord.
source: In general, the specification of OLs depends on SHH protein released from the notochord and floor plate, as Shh expression is both necessary and sufficient for OL generation in the spinal cord (Orentas et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Orentas et al., 1999.

claim: OL generation in the cortex is also dependent on the Shh signaling pathway.
source: As in the spinal cord, OL generation in the cortex is also dependent on the Shh signaling pathway (Lu et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2000.

claim: During MGE development, Nkx2.1 and Six3 promote SHH secretion.
source: During MGE development, Nkx2.1 and Six3 promote SHH secretion.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MGE development.

claim: The early-born neurons of the MGE also secrete SHH protein before E14.5.
source: Furthermore, the early-born neurons of the MGE also secrete SHH protein before E14.5 (Flandin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Flandin et al., 2011.

claim: The high levels of SHH in the MGE contribute to the generation of OPCs from RGCs.
source: Thus, the high levels of SHH in the MGE contribute to the generation of OPCs from RGCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the role of SHH in OPC specification.

claim: Shh signaling pathway activity is very weak in the LGE at the early stage (before E14.5).
source: In contrast, Shh signaling pathway activity is very weak in the LGE at the early stage (before E14.5).
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to the MGE, representing knowledge about LGE development.

claim: As the level of SHH gradually increases in the LGE, this results in a shift from neurogenesis to gliogenesis after E15.5.
source: As the level of SHH gradually increases in the LGE, this results in a shift from neurogenesis to gliogenesis after E15.5, and the large number of the striatal neurons may block the migration of OPCs into the neocortex (Tong et al., 2015; Su et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tong et al., 2015 and Su et al., 2022.

claim: The large number of the striatal neurons may block the migration of OPCs into the neocortex.
source: As the level of SHH gradually increases in the LGE, this results in a shift from neurogenesis to gliogenesis after E15.5, and the large number of the striatal neurons may block the migration of OPCs into the neocortex (Tong et al., 2015; Su et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism preventing OPC migration, supported by citations to Tong et al., 2015 and Su et al., 2022.

claim: The high level of SHH in the MGE allows for the production of a small population of cortical OPCs around E12.5.
source: First, the high level of SHH in the MGE allows for the production of a small population of cortical OPCs around E12.5.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating knowledge about SHH signaling and OPC generation.

claim: Multipotent intermediate progenitors begin to express DLX transcription factors resulting in ending the generation of OPCs in the MGE.
source: Subsequently, multipotent intermediate progenitors begin to express DLX transcription factors resulting in ending the generation of OPCs in the MGE (Dai et al., 2015; Silbereis et al., 2014; Price et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dai et al., 2015; Silbereis et al., 2014; and Price et al., 2022.

claim: RGCs undergo a gradual transition from neurogenesis to gliogenesis around E15.5, driven by the progressive elevation of SHH levels in the LGE.
source: Second, RGCs undergo a gradual transition from neurogenesis to gliogenesis around E15.5, driven by the progressive elevation of SHH levels in the LGE.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating knowledge about developmental transitions in the LGE.

claim: The LGE had already generated a substantial number of neurons during this period, blocking the migration of OPCs into the cortex.
source: However, the LGE had already generated a substantial number of neurons during this period, blocking the migration of OPCs into the cortex.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism preventing OPC migration from the LGE to cortex.

claim: Cortical RGCs begin to cease neurogenesis and shift toward gliogenesis after E16.5.
source: Finally, with the gradual increase of SHH concentration, cortical RGCs begin to cease neurogenesis and shift toward gliogenesis after E16.5 (Li et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2015; Winkler et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2021; Tong et al., 2015; and Winkler et al., 2018.

claim: The generation of cortical OPCs is regulated by both precise temporal and spatial patterning, which is strictly dependent on the local environment.
source: Therefore, the generation of cortical OPCs is regulated by both precise temporal and spatial patterning, which is strictly dependent on the local environment.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the discussion of developmental mechanisms.

claim: Most of the ventral-derived OPCs, particularly MGE-derived OPCs/OLs, are eventually eliminated due to the continued expansion of dorsal-derived OPCs in the adult cortex.
source: Interestingly, most of the ventral-derived OPCs, particularly MGE-derived OPCs/OLs, are eventually eliminated due to the continued expansion of dorsal-derived OPCs in the adult cortex (Liu et al., 2021; Kessaris et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2021 and Kessaris et al., 2006.

claim: OPCs generated later in development may possess a competitive advantage over their earlier-generated counterparts.
source: It appears that OPCs generated later in development may possess a competitive advantage over their earlier-generated counterparts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that later-generated OPCs replace earlier ones.

claim: Human glial progenitor cells engrafted neonatally or transplanted into the adult mouse brain can effectively disperse throughout the forebrain, differentiate into mature OLs, and remyelinate the demyelinated adult brain.
source: Indeed, human glial progenitor cells engrafted neonatally or transplanted into the adult mouse brain can effectively disperse throughout the forebrain, differentiate into mature OLs, and remyelinate the demyelinated adult brain (Goldman et al., 2021; Windrem et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goldman et al., 2021 and Windrem et al., 2020.

claim: OPCs generated later in development have the ability to take over for earlier-generated OPCs in the adult brain.
source: These findings indicate that OPCs generated later in development have the ability to take over for earlier-generated OPCs in the adult brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on transplantation studies.

claim: Cortical-derived OPCs probably constitute the majority of cortical OPCs, including mature cortical OLs.
source: Based on the present work and other studies (Marques et al., 2018; Kessaris et al., 2006; van Tilborg et al., 2018), cortical-derived OPCs probably constitute the majority of cortical OPCs, including mature cortical OLs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study and supported by citations to Marques et al., 2018; Kessaris et al., 2006; and van Tilborg et al., 2018.

claim: OLs may function as a homogeneous population in the adult forebrain.
source: Thus, OLs may function as a homogeneous population in the adult forebrain.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the predominance of cortical-derived OPCs in the adult brain.

claim: The number of LGE/CGE-derived cortical OPCs may also gradually decrease in the adult brain.
source: In fact, the number of LGE/CGE-derived cortical OPCs may also gradually decrease in the adult brain, as reported by Liu et al., 2021.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claim: Cortical OPCs/OLs comprise MGE-derived and cortical RGC-derived OPCs/OLs during the neonatal stage.
source: In summary, cortical OPCs/OLs comprise MGE-derived and cortical RGC-derived OPCs/OLs during the neonatal stage.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Cortical-derived OPCs/OLs make up the majority of the cortical OPCs/OLs in the adult cortex.
source: In contrast, cortical-derived OPCs/OLs make up the majority of the cortical OPCs/OLs in the adult cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and literature.

claim: Ventral-derived OLs contribution to cortex is minimal.
source: Recently, another study showed that ventral-derived OLs contribution to cortex is minimal.
evidence: This is mentioned as supporting evidence from another recent study.

claim: OPCs initially emerge in the ventral VZ of the MGE and can be labeled by platelet-derived growth factor receptor (α-subunit, Pdgfra) around E12.5.
source: OPCs initially emerge in the ventral VZ of the MGE and can be labeled by platelet-derived growth factor receptor (α-subunit, Pdgfra) around E12.5.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about OPC emergence and markers.

claim: If the LGE generated cortical OPCs, the Pdgfra+ cell migration stream from the LGE to the cortex could be observed during cortical development.
source: We hypothesized that if the LGE generated cortical OPCs, the Pdgfra+ cell migration stream from the LGE to the cortex could be observed during cortical development.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that was tested in the study.

claim: Both pallium and subpallium can generate cortical OPCs during the early development of the cortex.
source: During the early development of the cortex, both pallium and subpallium can generate cortical OPCs (Kessaris et al., 2006; van Tilborg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kessaris et al., 2006 and van Tilborg et al., 2018.

claim: The percentage of LGE/dMGE-derived cortical OPCs was approximately 3% at P10.
source: The pie chart shows that the percentage of LGE/dMGE-derived cortical OPCs was approximately 3%. N=6 mice per group.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The percentage of LGE/dMGE-derived cortical OPCs was less than 3% at P0.
source: The pie chart shows that the percentage of LGE/dMGE-derived cortical OPCs was less than 3%. N=6 mice per group.
